newsitem.title: USA: New York jury deliberating "moshing" death.
newsitem.headline: New York jury deliberating "moshing" death.

text.p: A New York City jury began deliberations Tuesday in the case of a nightclub bouncer accused in the "moshing" death of teenager at a rock conert.

The case, involving possibly the nation's first "moshing" fatality, concentrates on the practice of concert goers slamming into each other or jumping on stage and diving into the "moshpit" of the crowd below.

Bouncer James Gheida, 41, was charged in the death of Christopher Mitchell, 18, of Pearl River, New York, who fractured his skull in December 1994 at a "Life of Agony" concert at the L'Amour club in the borough of Brooklyn.
Prosecutors say Gheida grabbed Mitchell as the teenager was about to jump from the stage into the crowd and threw him headfirst into an unoccupied area of the dance floor.
Gheida was charged with manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide. If convicted of the weightiest charge he faces a possible 15 years in prison.

Defence attorneys produced two witnesses at the trial, who testified Gheida was not on stage when the incident occurred. They also introduced an autopsy report showing the teenager had consumed alcohol and had cocaine and barbituates in his system.

Mitchell's judgment was impaired and he "took a chance" when he jumped off the stage "and depended on the crowd to break his fall," defence attorney Barry Kenyon said Monday in closing arguments, adding, "There is no doubt that this was a death that was needless."
Gheida took the witness stand and denied throwing Mitchell to the floor.
But three of Mitchell's friends identified the bouncer and said he had tossed Mitchell to his death.
"The fact that he had drugs in his system ... that he had alcohol in his system has nothing to do his death," said prosecutor Edward Boyar in his closing argument.

"What caused his death was being pushed from behind from a height when he wasn't expecting it," Boyar said. "Had he been more sober, maybe he might have been able to recover in time to protect himself."
